The Plushcap (Catamblyrhynchus diadema) is a small, enigmatic passerine found in the montane cloud forests of the Andes, from Venezuela to Bolivia. Its distinctive yellow forehead patch contrasts sharply with its otherwise rufous and slate-gray plumage. Ecological data for this species remain relatively sparse, but recent field studies have begun to quantify key life-history parameters. Eggs are typically incubated at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], a temperature that appears to be optimal for embryonic development in this high-altitude environment, and the incubation period culminates in hatching after 12 days [ab = 12 days]. The newly emerged nestling, or hatchling, is altricial and weighs only 1.79 grams [Ww0 = 1.79 grams], a modest initial mass that underscores the profound parental investment required to reach independence. This low neonatal mass is typical of small-bodied passerines that produce altricial young, and it sets the stage for a rapid growth trajectory within the secure confines of a woven cup nest.

Under the typical thermal regime of an active breeding adult, measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the developmental milestones of the nestling period proceed in a predictable sequence. The young bird gains strength and develops its flight feathers, achieving its first flight—fledging—at 13 days after hatching [tx = 13 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This is a relatively short nestling period compared to many temperate passerines, likely an adaptation to the high predation pressure and unpredictable weather characteristic of tropical montane forests. Following nest departure, the fledgling enters a period of continued development. The attainment of sexual maturity, or puberty, occurs much later than fledging; available data indicate that individuals first reach puberty at 51 days after hatching [tp = 51 days after hatching] when maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This period of post-fledging development allows the juvenile bird to complete somatic growth.

The species' reproductive strategy appears to be conservative, typical of many tropical resident birds that face relatively stable but resource-limited environments. Females typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], a low annual frequency that limits the total number of offspring. Each clutch consists of 2 eggs [N_R_i = Each clutch consists of 2 eggs]. Combining these two parameters yields an annual reproductive output of just two eggs per year per breeding female, a value that reflects the high per-capita investment required to rear each nestling to independence in a challenging environment. The first successful breeding attempt in a female's life is deferred for some time; records indicate that the time since birth at first brood is 365 days [tR = 365 days] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This first reproduction occurs nearly a full year after hatching.

Adult body mass in the Plushcap shows a modest degree of sexual size dimorphism, a pattern common in many Andean passerines where males are slightly heavier than females. The maximum adult body mass attained by females is 13.4 grams [Wwi = 13.4 grams], whereas males reach a slightly greater ultimate wet weight of 14.9 grams [Wwi = 14.9 grams]. This difference, amounting to roughly 1.5 grams, is likely linked to the energetic demands of egg production in females versus the competitive demands of male-male interactions for territories and mates. The metabolic machinery that powers these activities is also well-characterized. Resting metabolic rate, measured via respirometry under controlled conditions, reaches a maximum of 45.45 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 45.45 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a value that is consistent with predictions for a bird of this small body size.

Longevity records for the Plushcap suggest a moderate lifespan for a tropical passerine of this mass. The maximum lifespan recorded in the wild, based on banding studies and re-sighting data, is approximately 7.4 years [am = approximately 7.4 years] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan, in comparison with many temperate-zone passerines of similar body size, is a common feature of tropical birds and is often interpreted as a consequence of lower extrinsic mortality rates and a slower pace of life. The low annual reproductive output of just 2 eggs per year, combined with a deferred age at first reproduction of one year, is consistent with this slow life-history strategy. The combination of a modest clutch size, a single annual breeding attempt, a relatively high adult survival rate, and a substantial lifespan allows the population to remain stable despite the production of few offspring each year.
